reviewer.origin: Claude Agent tool subagent, model sonnet, a fresh context with only this brief and its files, launched 2026-10-26 by session_01Mxpoi6tFT3FgKmBvtGjRtS (the writer's session)

evidence: Read cold in “Working with your guards”, in the paragraph that begins “Instead, you might feel numb, cynical, angry, hungry…”. The sentence before the draft is “It's what protects you when your consciously installed parental Protector isn't functioning, the same as when you were a child.” The draft follows as the next step: “Before figuring out what/where it is, make sure to ask what it is trying to stop or what it wants. It may, of course, be your inner child, mad that it’s taken you so long to come back, or it may be your inherited parent script, or something from earlier in the day, or a bit of each.” Pronouns: “it” in both sentences is the reaction or guard the paragraph has been describing (the numbness, the urges, “a very charming guard”), the same thing the next paragraph speaks to as “the guard” (“What's going on?”); “it’s taken you so long” is the ordinary impersonal “it has taken you”, and “come back” is the card’s own phrase for coming back to the inner child. Against the change: two sentences; ask what it is trying to stop or wants before deciding what it is; the child, the script, the day or a mix; and the last words are the approved card’s “or a bit of each”. Against SOURCE.txt (IC-A14: “But before you decide where it's coming from, ask it what it's trying to stop, or what it wants. It could also be your inner child, mad that you took so long to come back, or your inherited parent script, or something from earlier today, or a bit of each.”): every point is kept, in the same order, and nothing is added that is a claim. The shifts are Emulate’s turns and I checked each for meaning. “where it's coming from” becomes “what/where it is”: the slash is a little clunky, but the list that follows answers both what it is and where it comes from, so the sense holds. “ask it” becomes “ask”: what is asked is plain from “what it is trying to stop”, and the next paragraph speaks to the guard directly. “But” is dropped: the sentence reads fine as the next step. “could also” becomes “may, of course,”: a stance word, not a fact; the paragraph before has the reader expecting to meet the inner child, so “of course” fits, and it matches his own commas in “It’s good to notice it, though,” and his “it might just be hunger, or…” in the section’s first paragraph. “earlier today” becomes “earlier in the day”: same. Linter B4/E15 list or packed sentence: accepted. The four possibilities are the approved card’s own list and none can be dropped without changing what he approved; they are not one flat run either: the child comes with why it is mad, “it may be” restarts the clause for the script, “something from earlier in the day” is loose, and “a bit of each” is the catch-all. Linter D9 follows the source order: accepted. It is a rewrite of his card’s two sentences, so his points come in his order by design; I checked T13 and T09 as the linter asks: the child “mad that it’s taken you so long to come back” is a noticing that gets extra weight, and the rest of the paragraph is untouched. Linter E125 list of three: accepted. The draft takes the label’s own second route (items of different shapes ending on a casual catch-all), the catch-all is his “or a bit of each”, and the card he approved needs all of its items. Tell rows: I went through T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 on these literal words in their context and found none PRESENT. The ones I looked at hardest: T07 (“of course” and “make sure to” are colloquial, but each comes from a real turn of the thought and is not stage direction between beats); T22 (it is an instruction, but one that carries a step with content, in a paragraph that has stance and humor); T15 (the draft is Emulate’s rewording of the card by design, but the swaps are plain words and not rarer synonyms, and the card’s own last words are put back); T02 (one instruction and one set of possibilities inside a longer paragraph, not a run of compressed commands); T12 and T21 (an open enumeration of what a reaction may be, not a closed taxonomy or several argumentative jobs); T29 (the last sentence adds the mixed case instead of restating); C01 (“your inner child”, never “the kid”); C03 and C04 (no first-person fact, no outside claim). Non-blocking notes: “what/where” is the one phrase an author might choose to change back to the card’s “where it's coming from”; “inherited parent script” is not explained in this section, but it is the card’s own term and the draft does not introduce it; the curly apostrophe in “it’s taken” sits among straight ones in the neighbouring sentences, which does not show in reading.
resolved_lint_labels: E125 list of three: an AI pattern in general (Joel 2026-10-03: "lists of 3 in general are an ai pattern"; 2026-10-07: "lists in general are overused by AI. try to avoid that unless it's really needed"). If the meaning doesn't need all three, drop the one that matters least; if it does, split them into sentences, the way he fixed P1 ("Maybe it just has something to say."), or give the items different shapes and end on a catch-all, the way he fixed Borrowed Adulthood P2 ("Other jobs can go to friends or community, outsource to the tools or pros, whatever works."). Joel, 01:06: "when there's no actual need for 3 items you can remove one of them"
